questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Given Time
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is moving in the $x$-$y$ plane. Its position vector relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-t,\,2{t}^{2}-4t+2⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-4t+2)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-4t-1,4t-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=2,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨3(2)^{2}-4(2)-1,4(2)-4⟩ \\  & =⟨3,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=2$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(2),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions at a Given Time
questions.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{4t+1},3t-2⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{4t+1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{\sqrt{4t+1}},3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=2,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨\frac{2}{\sqrt{4(2)+1}},3⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{\sqrt{9}},3⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Given Time
questions.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=\pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=\pi ,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\pi ) & =⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨-4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=\pi $ we calculate the magnitude of $v(\pi ),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(\pi )| & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+0} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed when $t=\pi $ is $4.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Times at Which a Particle Is Stationary
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
r=⟨{t}^{2}-6t,(t-3)^{5}⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-6t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t-3)^{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-6,5(t-3)^{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨2(t-3),5(t-3)^{4}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2(t-3),5(t-3)^{4}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t-3)=0\, & ⇒\,t=3, \\ 5(t-3)^{4}=0\, & ⇒\,t=3.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=3$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

questions.problem:

$$
r=⟨\frac{3(t-2)^{2}}{t+1},\frac{3(t-2)^{2}}{t+5}⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.

{{field-1}}.

First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3(t-2)^{2}}{t+1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3(t-2)^{2}}{t+5})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3(t-2)(t+4)}{(t+1)^{2}},\frac{3(t-2)(t+12)}{(t+5)^{2}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{3(t-2)(t+4)}{(t+1)^{2}},\frac{3(t-2)(t+12)}{(t+5)^{2}}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3(t-2)(t+4)}{(t+1)^{2}}=0\, & ⇒\,3(t-2)(t+4)=0\,⇒\,t=2,-4, \\ \frac{3(t-2)(t+12)}{(t+5)^{2}}=0\, & ⇒\,3(t-2)(t+12)=0\,⇒\,t=2,-12.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=2$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.
